content: Horseradish, scientifically known as Armoracia rusticana (synonym Cochlearia armoracia), is a perennial plant belonging to the Brassicaceae family, which also includes mustard, wasabi, and cabbages. It is believed to have originated in southeastern Europe and western Asia, but it is now cultivated and enjoyed globally. The plant can grow up to five feet tall and is primarily cultivated for its large, white, tapered root. The root itself has little to no aroma in its intact state. However, when it is cut or grated, enzymes from the damaged plant cells break down a glucosinolate compound called sinigrin, producing allyl isothiocyanate (commonly known as mustard oil). This compound is responsible for the characteristic pungency of horseradish, which can irritate the sinuses and eyes. If the grated root is not used immediately or preserved in vinegar, it darkens, loses its pungency, and develops an unpleasantly bitter taste when exposed to air and heat. History Horseradish has been cultivated since antiquity. According to Greek mythology, the Delphic Oracle once told Apollo that horseradish was worth its weight in gold. The plant was known in Egypt as early as 1500 BCE and has been traditionally used by Eastern European Jews during Passover Seders. Roman agriculturalist Cato mentioned the plant in his writings, and a mural in Pompeii depicting horseradish has survived to this day. Pliny the Elder referred to it as Amoracia in his Natural History, recommending it for its medicinal properties. It may also have been the wild radish (raphanos agrios) described by the Greeks. During the Middle Ages, both the root and leaves were used medicinally, and the root became a popular condiment for meats in Germany, Scandinavia, and Britain. It was introduced to North America during the Colonial period. William Turner mentioned horseradish as Red Cole in his Herbal (1551–1568), though not as a condiment. John Gerard, in his Herball (1597), described it as raphanus rusticanus, noting its wild occurrence in parts of England and its use among Germans as a sauce for fish and meats, similar to mustard. Cultivation Horseradish is a hardy perennial in USDA zones 2–9 and can be grown as an annual in other zones, though it thrives best in regions with a long growing season and cold winters to ensure plant dormancy. After the first frost in autumn kills the leaves, the root is harvested and divided. The main root is collected, while one or more large offshoots are replanted to produce the next year's crop. If left undisturbed, horseradish spreads via underground shoots and can become invasive. Older roots left in the ground become woody and lose their culinary value, though they can still be divided to propagate new plants. Pests and Diseases Imported cabbage worms (Artogeia rapae) are a common pest affecting horseradish. The adult form is a white butterfly with black spots on its forewings, often seen flying around plants during the day. The caterpillars are velvety green with faint yellow stripes running lengthwise along their backs and sides. Fully grown caterpillars reach about one inch in length and move sluggishly when disturbed. They overwinter in green pupal cases and emerge as adults after the last frost, remaining a problem throughout the growing season. There are typically 3–5 overlapping generations per year. Mature caterpillars chew large, ragged holes in the leaves, leaving the main veins intact. Handpicking is an effective control method. Commercial Production Collinsville, Illinois, is known as the Horseradish Capital of the World and hosts an annual International Horseradish Festival each June. The region produces 60% of the world's commercially grown horseradish, with the surrounding area of southwestern Illinois accounting for 85%. Other major horseradish-growing regions in the United States include Wisconsin and northern California. Culinary Uses The grated root of the horseradish plant, often mixed with vinegar, is referred to as prepared horseradish. It is white to creamy beige in color and can be refrigerated for months, though it will eventually darken and lose its flavor, signaling the need for replacement. The leaves, while edible, are not commonly consumed and are known as horseradish greens. Although technically a root, horseradish is primarily used as a condiment or ingredient. In the United States, prepared horseradish is a common ingredient in Bloody Mary cocktails, cocktail sauce, and as a spread or sauce for meats, chicken, fish, and sandwiches. The fast-food chain Arby’s incorporates horseradish into its Horsey Sauce, a regular condiment alongside ketchup, mustard, and mayonnaise. This practice is uncommon among its competitors. Several manufacturers produce prepared horseradish in the U.S., with one company alone producing 5 million jars annually. In the United Kingdom, horseradish sauce made from grated root and cream is a popular condiment, often served with roast beef but also used in other dishes. Tewkesbury mustard, a blend of mustard and grated horseradish, originated in medieval times and was mentioned by Shakespeare. In Eastern European Jewish cuisine, a sweetened horseradish-vinegar sauce called chrain traditionally accompanies gefilte fish. There are two varieties: red chrain, mixed with red beet, and white chrain, which contains no beet. Horseradish is also popular in Poland (chrzan), Hungary (torma), Romania (hrean), and Bulgaria (хрян), where it is a traditional part of Easter celebrations. In Poland, a variety mixed with red beet is called ćwikła z chrzanem or simply ćwikła. In Slovenia and the Italian region of Friuli Venezia Giulia, horseradish (often grated and mixed with cream, hardboiled eggs, or apples) is a traditional Easter dish. In Poland's Silesia region, horseradish soup is a main dish on Easter Sunday. Additionally, horseradish dyed green is often used as a substitute for the more expensive wasabi traditionally served with sushi, even in Japan. The Japanese botanical name for horseradish is Western wasabi. Horseradish owes its pungent taste to two glucosinolates, sinigrin and gluconasturtiin. Nutritional Value Horseradish is a source of potassium, calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus. It also contains volatile oils, such as mustard oil, which has antibiotic properties. It provides 31 mg of vitamin C per 100 grams of raw horseradish. Research Applications The enzyme horseradish peroxidase (HRP), found in the plant, is widely used in molecular biology, particularly for antibody detection. It plays a significant role in immunohistochemistry (IHC), a branch of human pathology. HRP is used to stain thin tissue biopsy slices (~5 micrometers) from patients suspected of having cancer. HRP molecules are bound to a polymer along with immunoglobulins that bind to a primary immunoglobulin recognizing a specific biomarker in the tissue. HRP converts 3,3-diaminobenzidine (DAB) into a yellowish-brown insoluble compound visible under a microscope, aiding pathologists in cancer diagnosis. HRP is also used in materials for detecting glucose in blood or urine. Medicinal Applications Horseradish roots are known for their diuretic properties and have been used to treat minor health issues such as urinary tract infections, bronchitis, sinus congestion, and coughs. Compounds in horseradish have demonstrated antibacterial activity against certain bacterial strains.
